items.title: Israel Cracks Down in West Bank City After Deadly Attack
items.summary: Hundreds of Palestinian families fled their homes as the Israeli military raided Hebron. The operation came a day after Palestinian gunmen killed two soldiers.
items.full_text:
Title: Israel Cracks Down in West Bank City After Deadly Attack - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/world/middleeast/israel-military-hebron-west-bank.html

Published Time: Sat, 24 Oct 2026 18:54:23 GMT

Markdown Content:
The Israeli military began a sweeping crackdown in the West Bank city of Hebron overnight on Saturday, evicting hundreds of families and demolishing buildings a day after Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers in the occupied territory.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had vowed to retaliate for the deadly shooting, which took place just days before a pivotal national election and against a [backdrop of intensifying violence](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/world/middleeast/west-bank-settlers-palestinians-harvest.html) in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. Mr. Netanyahu is [neck and neck in opinion polls](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/world/middleeast/netanyahu-has-reinvented-himself-will-voters-think-its-enough.html) with a bloc led by [Gadi Eisenkot](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/world/middleeast/gadi-eisenkot-israel-election.html), a former military chief of staff and his leading challenger in the first major vote in Israel since the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks ignited the war in Gaza.

On Saturday, Israeli forces were searching homes, making arrests and using loudspeakers to tell residents in Hebron’s Deir Baha neighborhood to leave, said Yousef Jabari, the city’s mayor. At least 2,000 Palestinians live in the area, many of whom have already fled, he said.

Image

Palestinians surveying their homes after the Israeli Army forced them to evacuate from the Deir Baha neighborhood in Hebron.Credit...John Wessels/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

“This is not only collective punishment, it’s election propaganda,” said Mr. Jabari. “Netanyahu wants images of displacement, destroyed buildings and repression to appeal to voters.”

Khaled Fahd Qawasmi, the deputy mayor, said more than 200 Palestinian families were believed to have been displaced since the operation began overnight.

The Israeli military said the raid would last for several days in response to the attack on Friday, in which [two Palestinians opened fire on Israeli troops](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/world/middleeast/israel-military-hebron-west-bank.html) near a checkpoint outside of Hebron. The gunmen were killed in a subsequent shootout, the military said.

Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, Israel’s military chief of staff, said in a statement that the soldiers had prevented “an even more serious attack.” The military said a large cache of ammunition was found in a vehicle used by the attackers.

The two shooters have not been officially identified, and it was unclear whether they acted alone or on behalf of a militant group. Hamas, the Palestinian armed group based in Gaza, praised the attack but stopped short of claiming responsibility for it.

Israeli forces quickly moved to encircle Hebron, the largest Palestinian city in the West Bank, sealing off the city’s main entrances and exits. Israel Katz, the defense minister, vowed to [replicate an operation in the cities of Tulkarm and Jenin](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/02/17/world/middleeast/west-bank-palestinian-displacement.html), where Israeli officials have occupied entire neighborhoods and displaced tens of thousands of people.

Image

Passing packages under a closed checkpoint gate at one of the entrances to Hebron on Saturday.Credit...John Wessels/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

Mr. Netanyahu and Mr. Katz said a similar campaign would be carried out in the two gunmen’s Hebron neighborhood. They did not specify the neighborhood, but Mr. Jabari said it was probably Deir Baha.

“We will evacuate the residents, we will go house to house, we will also confiscate the weapons there, and all terrorist infrastructures will be dealt with and destroyed,” Mr. Netanyahu said.

The Israeli military said Palestinian civilians would be allowed to leave through designated checkpoints but did not say whether they would be permitted to return. An Israeli military spokesman did not respond to a request for comment.

Violence in the West Bank has been escalating lately. In recent weeks, extremist Jewish settlers have initiated dozens of attacks against Palestinians during the annual olive harvest, a cultural touchstone for many Palestinians. Masked Israelis have assaulted Palestinians gathering olives, beating them with clubs and hurling stones.

The heightened strife comes just days before an Israeli election that Israelis and [Palestinians](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/21/world/middleeast/stakes-for-palestinians-of-israel-election.html), who cannot vote in it, view as [existential](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/world/middleeast/israel-october-7-attacks-elections.html). Mr. Netanyahu, who has led the most hard-line, right-wing government in Israeli history, is fighting for his political life.

Video

[Video 3](https://vp.nyt.com/video/hlsfmp4/2026/10/23/181613_1_23vid-hebron-attack_wg_mobile_av1-1080p/master.m3u8)

![Image 1](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/23/multimedia/23int-westbank-shooting-01-vthm/23int-westbank-shooting-01-vthm-videoLarge-v2.jpg?auto=webp&quality=30&disable=upscale&format=pjpg)Palestinian Gunmen Kill Two Israeli Soldiers in the West Bank

0:57

Two Israeli soldiers were killed after Palestinians opened fire in the West Bank on Friday. The Israeli military said it killed two assailants, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned of a major offensive in the occupied West Bank.Credit Credit...Ammar Awad/Reuters

Some Israeli analysts have said the vote may be influencing the prime minister’s decision to start a major military operation in the West Bank. Both Mr. Netanyahu and his opponents have sought to burnish their security credentials to woo Israeli voters rattled by three years of war.

Israeli forces also began razing buildings near the scene of the attack in the Farsh al-Hawa neighborhood on the western outskirts of Hebron. The Israeli military said it was “demolishing illegal structures that could pose a security threat.”

Image

A Palestinian man cleared debris outside a business in Hebron that was demolished by the Israeli Army.Credit...John Wessels/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

One of the houses belonged to Riyad Mreish, a Palestinian who spent more than two decades working in Saudi Arabia. Mr. Mreish said he had poured the savings he had accumulated during his time abroad into the home.

“I haven’t slept a moment,” Mr. Mreish said. “I cannot comprehend what happened.”

Israel regularly demolishes Palestinian homes in West Bank areas under its direct control, arguing that they were built illegally. Palestinians say Israel almost never issues Palestinians any permits for legal construction, forcing them to build without them.

Heedo Abu Laban and Adam Rasgon contributed reporting.

items.title: Netanyahu Is Up for Re-election After Years of War. How Will Voters See Him?
items.summary: The Oct. 7 attacks marred Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s image as Mr. Security. Ahead of elections, he’s trying to sell Israelis on the new, hawkish version of himself.
items.full_text:
Title: Netanyahu Is Up for Re-election After Years of War. How Will Voters See Him? - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/world/middleeast/netanyahu-has-reinvented-himself-will-voters-think-its-enough.html

Published Time: Sat, 24 Oct 2026 19:21:40 GMT

Markdown Content:
Benjamin Netanyahu looks thinner and paler these days. Gone is the swagger of previous political campaigns. But he remains tireless, traipsing among shopping centers and television studios, trying to persuade a weary and polarized country to return him to office for up to another four years in Israeli elections on Tuesday.

At 77, he is already Israel’s longest-serving prime minister. If he is to extend that tenure, he has to sell the deeply divided electorate on the new, more hawkish version of himself — and of Israel.

Mr. Netanyahu’s career will forever be defined by the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel, the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust. He long had a reputation for being risk averse and avoiding military confrontations, even as he cultivated an image as Israel’s Mr. Security. But that image, as well as Israel’s confidence in its own defense, was badly damaged that day.

So Mr. Netanyahu, known by friends and foes as Bibi, reinvented himself. Instead of sticking to Israel’s previous security doctrine centered on short wars of defense, he has waged Israel’s longest war on multiple fronts — against Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah militants in Lebanon, the Houthi militia in Yemen and, together with the United States, Iran.

He has doubled down on Israel’s occupation of the West Bank, allowing Jewish settlements [to proliferate](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2025/12/20/world/middleeast/west-bank-settlements.html) and settler violence against Palestinians [to escalate](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/world/middleeast/israel-west-bank-settlers-palestinians.html), further aggravating Israel’s international isolation.

“He understood that if he wanted to survive, not only politically but as a historic figure, he had to change,” said Mazal Mualem, an Israeli political commentator and Netanyahu biographer. “He killed off the old Bibi and delivered a new one into the world,” she added.

Image

![Image 1: A man in a dark jacket and tie stands behind a podium, holding up both his hands, palms open.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/22/multimedia/xxint-israel-netanyahu-profile-01-kzjq/xxint-israel-netanyahu-profile-01-kzjq-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Mr. Netanyahu giving a victory speech in 1996 after being elected prime minister of Israel for the first time. Credit...Jim Hollander/Reuters

After the Oct. 7 attacks, Mr. Netanyahu promised total victory over Hamas and other enemies. While Israel’s military campaign has left those adversaries battered, the wars have been inconclusive. Now, he says there is more to be done, and that he is the one to do it. “We must complete the elimination of the Iranian regime,” he said on Tuesday.

It is unclear whether he will get the chance. Days before what many Israelis view as the most fateful election in the country’s history, Mr. Netanyahu and his Likud party are in a tight race against an opposition led by [Gadi Eisenkot, a centrist and former military chief](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/world/middleeast/gadi-eisenkot-israel-election.html). Opinion polls show the opposition slightly ahead but lacking enough seats to guarantee a governing coalition.

Mr. Netanyahu may have lost some of his luster, but he is a master politician who has maintained a loyal base of supporters and cultivated strong political alliances, meaning that he cannot be counted out.

## A Question of Responsibility

As prime minister for most of the past 17 years, in addition to a three-year term in the 1990s, Mr. Netanyahu has evolved along with the Israel he has largely shaped.

He returned to power in late 2022 after a brief hiatus. Shunned by other mainstream parties because he [faces corruption charges](https://www.nytimes.com/article/netanyahu-corruption-trial-pardon.html), Mr. Netanyahu formed a governing coalition with the participation of far-right extremists who had been considered beyond the pale by most Israeli politicians.

At the time, he told Israel’s Parliament that the country was in its “golden age” after “the quietest and safest security decade in our history.” Even as he repeated a pledge to block Iran from developing a nuclear weapon, he trumpeted his aim to “widen the circle of peace” with the goal of ending the Arab-Israeli conflict.

Instead, on the morning of Oct. 7, 2023, thousands of gunmen surged across the border from Gaza, overrunning [Israeli communities](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2023/12/22/world/europe/beeri-massacre.html), [army bases](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/12/30/world/middleeast/israeli-military-hamas-failures.html) and [a music festival](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/05/13/world/middleeast/israel-oct-7-nova-festival-memorial-day.html), killing about 1,200 people, according to the Israeli authorities, and taking 251 hostages.

Image

Friends of Yam Goldstein mourning the deaths of her and her father, Nadav Goldstein, during their funeral in Shefayim, Israel, in October 2023. They were killed in Kfar Aza, Israel, on Oct. 7.Credit...Tamir Kalifa for The New York Times

Mr. Netanyahu has not taken personal responsibility for government failures that preceded the attacks, including his policy aimed at [fostering quiet](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/12/10/world/middleeast/israel-qatar-money-prop-up-hamas.html?eafs_enabled=false) in Hamas-run Gaza rather than confronting the militant group, or the military and intelligence lapses that left Israel vulnerable. He has blocked an independent state inquiry into what went wrong.

Mr. Netanyahu says that his security chiefs chose not to wake him on Oct. 7.

But Mr. Netanyahu and Israeli security leaders repeatedly downplayed [signs](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/02/27/world/middleeast/israel-military-hamas-oct-7.html) that Gaza militants were gearing up for an assault, including reports of heightened Hamas activity from [female military spotters](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/01/25/world/middleeast/israel-spotters-hostages.html) and the acquisition of [a Hamas battle plan](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/11/30/world/middleeast/israel-hamas-attack-intelligence.html).

## A New Doctrine

Israel’s war against Hamas killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza health officials, prompting accusations of war crimes against Mr. Netanyahu from rights groups and foreign governments.

Critics and former Israeli officials also say he [prolonged the war](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/07/11/magazine/benjamin-netanyahu-gaza-war.html) in Gaza, which Israel launched in response to the Oct. 7 attacks, and delayed deals for the release of hostages — to keep his far-right coalition partners on board and remain in power. The prime minister’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

The wars have also overstretched the military and taken a toll on many Israelis, who have performed repeated tours as reserve soldiers. At the same time, Mr. Netanyahu has extended the exemption of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men from mandatory military service, bending to the demands of his ultra-Orthodox coalition partners who say religious study is a higher priority.

Israel’s conduct in the Gaza war has also [left the country increasingly isolated](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/10/12/world/middleeast/israel-us-polls-support.html) and facing international boycotts and embargoes. Although Mr. Netanyahu, who spent part of his childhood in Pennsylvania, prides himself on speaking “American,” support for Israel in the United States is at an unprecedented low, said Daniel B. Shapiro, a former U.S. ambassador to Israel.

“There’s no way you could reverse that without a change in leadership, in the face of Israel,” he added.

Mr. Netanyahu’s vision of an Israeli Sparta — an insular, self-sufficient, militaristic society — which he offered at an economic conference in 2025, has been deeply unsettling for many Israelis, who have traditionally enjoyed economic and other ties overseas.

In the past, Mr. Netanyahu was loath to preside over an open-ended war. “I am not eager for unnecessary wars,” he said in 2018 amid tensions along the Gaza border, adding that he was working to ease the economic crisis in the enclave to prevent an escalation in violence.

Image

Palestinians inspecting the site of an Israeli strike in Gaza City, Gaza, in July.Credit...Saher Alghorra for The New York Times

For a quarter-century, mostly under Mr. Netanyahu, Israel lived largely within its border fences after withdrawing from southern Lebanon in 2000 and from Gaza in 2005.

Now, saying it is acting to protect Israeli border communities, Israel is again occupying swaths of territory in Lebanon and Gaza, and expanded the area it occupies in Syria. Military policies of containment have been set aside. On Sunday, Mr. Netanyahu published his updated national security doctrine, putting a priority on pre-empting threats.

After Israel [killed Hezbollah’s longtime leader](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/09/28/world/middleeast/hassan-nasrallah-hezbollah-dead.html) in Lebanon, in 2024, Mr. Netanyahu summed up his philosophy by invoking a Talmudic teaching on pre-emptive action. “If someone rises up to kill you,” he said, “kill him first.”

## ‘King of Israel’

On the campaign trail, Mr. Netanyahu continues to sound an alert about what he deems threats external and internal, stoking fear of Israel’s Arab citizens and questioning the legitimacy of the political parties that represent them.

On a recent weeknight, security officers ushered Mr. Netanyahu into a grimy food court at a shopping mall in Holon, a Tel Aviv suburb. About 200 people were waiting for him.

“Bibi, King of Israel!” the crowd chanted, repeating a common refrain.

items.title: Six Flags to Add Seatbelts on Roller Coasters After Rider’s Death
items.summary: The company said that all Six Flags rides and attractions would undergo safety reviews, as the park operator faces lawsuits over safety concerns.
items.full_text:
Title: Six Flags to Add Seatbelts on Roller Coasters After Rider’s Death - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/business/six-flags-death-roller-coaster-seat-belt.html

Published Time: Sat, 24 Oct 2026 19:21:42 GMT

Markdown Content:
Six Flags will add seatbelts to select roller coasters across its parks, the company said on Friday, weeks after the death of a man who fell from a ride at one of its properties.

The announcement came as Six Flags contended with [recent lawsuits](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/23/us/six-flags-x2-roller-coaster-injuries.html) over safety concerns.

John Reilly, the president of Six Flags Entertainment Corporation, said in a statement on Friday that the company’s parks hired independent engineers and inspectors to conduct safety reviews of all rides and attractions as the additional safety measures were put in place.

“We are committed to carefully evaluating their findings and taking appropriate action to further strengthen our standards and culture of safety,” Mr. Reilly said in the statement.

Earlier this month, Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, was [thrown from his seat](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/us/roller-coaster-georgia-six-flags-rider-death.html) and declared dead after riding Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia in Austell, Ga., the state’s tallest roller coaster. That ride is temporarily closed and will receive seatbelts when it reopens.

Goliath was previously equipped with the commonly used lap-bar “clamshell” restraints, which swing down to lock above the riders’ laps.

State authorities, as well as the Cobb County Police Department, [are investigating](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/us/six-flags-roller-coaster-death.html) the death, but there is no single federal agency responsible for enforcing safety standards for rides like Goliath, which had passed its most recent state inspection on March 16.

The other attractions that will receive the safety additions are Nitro at Six Flags Great Adventure in Jackson, N.J., and Raging Bull at Six Flags Great America in Gurnee, Ill., which is north of Chicago, a spokeswoman for the company said in an email on Saturday.

Aside from Goliath, eight rides at five other parks are temporarily closed, Mr. Reilly said in his statement.

Ride safety at Six Flags parks has come under intense scrutiny over the past several weeks, even before Mr. Kariem’s death.

In September, three people sued the amusement park company and the ride’s manufacturer after suffering what they said were catastrophic brain injuries from riding the X2 coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Southern California. The lawsuits accuse Six Flags and a manufacturer of X2’s parts of operating a defectively designed ride and failing to adequately warn passengers about the risk of serious brain injuries.

That month, Six Flags Magic Mountain said the X2 would [permanently close](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/six-flags-magic-mountain-x2-roller-coaster-closed.html).

Before those lawsuits, Mr. Reilly said during an August call with analysts that the company incurred higher repair and maintenance expenses at certain parks as it reduced downtime, adding, “We will not compromise on safety.”

In its [second-quarter financial filings](https://investors.sixflags.com/news/press-releases/press-release-details/2026/Six-Flags-Entertainment-Corporation-Reports-2026-Second-Quarter-Results/default.aspx), released in August, Six Flags reported that its net revenue was $865 million, a decrease of $65 million from the same time last year. Attendance for the quarter was just above 13 million visits, a decrease from more than 14 million for the same period in 2025.

There are currently more than 220 coasters operating across all Six Flags parks, Mr. Reilly said on Friday.

“We will continue to communicate about our progress and hold ourselves accountable to our commitments to you,” he said.

items.title: Noah Adams, Longtime Host of ‘All Things Considered,’ Has Died at 84
items.summary: A postman’s son from Kentucky, he worked hard to lose his accent but never forgot his Appalachian roots. “The best stories come from west of the Potomac,” he said.
items.full_text:
Title: Noah Adams, Longtime Host of ‘All Things Considered,’ Has Died at 84 - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/business/media/noah-adams-dead.html

Published Time: Sat, 24 Oct 2026 19:07:59 GMT

Markdown Content:
Noah Adams, a longtime host of NPR’s “All Things Considered” whose quiet baritone and empathetic ear brought listeners stories of back-roads America not often heard on the national airwaves, died on Oct. 16 at his home in Yellow Springs, Ohio. He was 84.

The cause was complications of a benign brain tumor removed eight years ago, his wife, Neenah Ellis, said.

Mr. Adams was a postman’s son from Kentucky who never finished college, and he worked hard to lose the Appalachian accent that he knew conjured up negative stereotypes about his native region.

But he never lost his respect for rural and working-class Americans, and he delighted in leaving Washington, where NPR is based, to travel around the country interviewing miners, farmers, single mothers and factory workers.

In the morning meetings, where the day’s events and newsmakers were discussed, Ms. Ellis, who worked in production at NPR, recalled, “He was looking for who was yearning, who was in pain, who needed help out in the country.”

Mr. Adams abhorred interviewing officials with pat talking points, though that was often part of his job as host of the weeknight edition of “All Things Considered,” NPR’s flagship news and interview show, a position he held for 18 years. He preferred to seek out regular people whose lives were affected by national events.

“The best stories come from west of the Potomac,” he once said.

Image

Mr. Adams, center, in 1996 with his “All Things Considered” co-hosts, Linda Wertheimer and Robert Siegel, who described him as “a very private and shy person.”Credit...Barbara Ries/NPR

His respect for his sources came through in interviews of those unaccustomed to a microphone.

“He was wonderfully warm and conversational with people,” said Melissa Block, another host of “All Things Considered,” who worked as a producer for Mr. Adams early in her career. “I don’t know that anyone talking with him would think, ‘Oh, the interview is about to start.’ It would just be a conversation.”

From 1982 to 1987, Mr. Adams’s co-host on “All Things Considered” was [Susan Stamberg](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/10/16/business/media/susan-stamberg-dead.html), an emotive, brainy New Yorker. It was a matchup that showed how opposites attract.

“He is the most genuine, uncontrived voice in broadcasting,” Ms. Stamberg wrote in the introduction to a 1992 book that Mr. Adams wrote about a year of his work for NPR.

After a short hiatus, he returned to host “All Things Considered” with Robert Siegel and Linda Wertheimer from 1989 until 2002.

“He was a very private and shy person,” Mr. Siegel said in an interview.

After Mr. Adams wrote a book about learning to play the piano at 51, “Piano Lessons” (1997), Mr. Siegel recalled Mr. Adams’s distress at realizing that he would have to perform on his book tour: “I watched him at a Borders, and he was terrified. But he loved what he did. He pulled it off very beautifully.”

During his time away from NPR, from 1987 to 1989, Mr. Adams was recruited to host a replacement show for the much-loved “A Prairie Home Companion,” whose creator, Garrison Keillor, had left. The replacement, “Good Evening,” was another folksy variety show broadcast live from a theater in St. Paul, Minn. It was enlivened by Mr. Adams’s essays about the community on the St. Croix River where he had settled, but it struggled to replicate Mr. Keillor’s audience.

The show lasted less than a year, and Mr. Adams announced his departure shortly before it ended. “I never felt people were saying, ‘Gee, that’s not Garrison Keillor,’” he later said somewhat defensively.

Noah Donald Adams was born on Sept. 15, 1942, in Ashland, Ky., the elder of fraternal twin boys. His father, Roy Adams, and his mother, Edith (Wellman) Adams, a secretary, divorced soon after, and Noah and his brother, James, were raised by their mother and maternal grandparents.

Noah graduated from Ashland High School (now Paul G. Blazer High School) and attended Eastern Kentucky State College (now Eastern Kentucky University) for 18 months before being asked to leave because he was living in unauthorized off-campus housing and writing term papers for football players.

He knocked around doing various jobs, — including construction and car sales, before joining the University of Kentucky’s public radio station, WBKY (now WUKY), in Lexington. There, he hosted a progressive rock show and worked the control board for other shows.

After writing a letter to NPR, he was hired in 1975 as a production assistant on “All Things Considered,” which had been introduced four years earlier. In 1978, he became a weekend co-host for the show.

A 90-minute documentary that he co-wrote about the mass suicide at Jonestown in Guyana in 1978, [“Father Cares: The Last of Jonestown”](https://www.npr.org/2016/10/18/497967228/father-cares-the-last-of-jonestown) (1981), received wide notice for its innovative format and subject. It was based on 900 hours of recordings that the cult leader Jim Jones and his followers had made before their deaths. Mr. Jones’s voice was so chilling, The Minneapolis Star Tribune noted, that “a listener might cling to the rational tone of narrator Noah Adams as to the hand of a friend.”

Though he preferred feature reporting, Mr. Adams did not shy away from hard news at home or abroad. He won an award from the Overseas Press Club of America in 1994 for work he did in Serbia on the roots of the country’s national extremism.

On Sept. 11, 2001, he was on the air from the morning until after dark, updating millions of listeners about the terrorist attacks. He called it the most important day of his career, when he could “feel the audience” intent on understanding the shocking events, Ms. Ellis said.

The following year, Mr. Adams took a leave of absence to research a book about the Wright brothers, one of five nonfiction books he wrote. When he returned, it was as a contributing correspondent on NPR’s national desk. He roamed widely but regularly returned to stories in Appalachia.

Image

Mr. Adams had “the most genuine, uncontrived voice in broadcasting,” Ms. Stamberg wrote in the introduction to his 1992 book about working at NPR.Credit...W.W. Norton & Company

Ms. Ellis, who married Mr. Adams in 1987, recalled visiting Appalachia for the first time with him. They were on assignment — she was his producer — and he instructed her and an engineer on how to approach strangers wary of outsiders. You don’t knock on their doors, he told them: “You drive up, get out of the car and stand there until they come out.”

Mr. Adams’s first two marriages ended in divorce. In addition to Ms. Ellis, he is survived by his brother.

Among the thousands of stories that Mr. Adams reported, the one that got the most enthusiastic response was when he visited a New York recording studio and [sang a wobbly version](https://www.npr.org/2008/11/21/97312511/taking-pitch-correction-to-the-limit) of the Eagles song “Take It to the Limit.”

He played the tape on the air for Ms. Stamberg, who squealed, “It’s adorable!”

One of the hundreds of listeners who wrote in said, “I was getting ready to drop out of law school and we were thinking about getting a divorce, but if you have the courage to stand in that studio and play it for Susan on the radio, then I know we can do anything we really set our minds to.”
